title: Testosterone and Estrogen: Wondrous Hormones
summary: Josh and Chuck examine the common view of estrogen as the female sex hormone and testosterone as the male sex hormone, arguing this binary picture is oversimplified. They trace the history from early 1900s animal experiments (Ernest Starling coining "hormone," Eugene Steinach's work, and critic Carl Moore), the discovery and marketing of estrogen drugs such as Premarin, the 2002 Women's Health Initiative study and its media overreporting, and the isolation and uses of testosterone. They describe the three main estrogens (estrone, estradiol, estriol), their roles beyond reproduction (bone, muscle, endurance, brain), the androgen family, prenatal hormone effects and aromatase, hormone levels across life stages, links between testosterone and behavior like aggression and winning or losing, and medical uses of hormone therapy, puberty blockers, and testosterone replacement. The episode closes with a listener email about the origin of yellow school buses and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open the episode with light banter about the show and introduce the topic of testosterone and estrogen.

segments.title: Rethinking the binary of estrogen and testosterone
segments.summary: The hosts argue that the popular notion of estrogen as female and testosterone as male is an oversimplification, and that the binary idea traces back to early experiments.

segments.title: Early hormone experiments and Eugene Steinach
segments.summary: Mid-nineteenth and early twentieth century animal experiments are described, including Ernest Starling coining the word hormone in 1905 and Eugene Steinach's gonad transplant work. Steinach's binary interpretation was challenged by embryologist Carl Moore. The hosts joke about the claim that Steinach had Moore murdered, which they say is not established.

segments.title: Estrogen drugs and Premarin
segments.summary: Early twentieth century isolation of estrogen and its use for menopause symptoms. Premarin, derived from pregnant mare urine, became a best-selling drug, and its popularity dropped around 2002.

segments.title: Women's Health Initiative and hormone therapy risk
segments.summary: The 2002 Women's Health Initiative study linked hormone therapy to breast cancer, heart disease, blood clots and stroke. The hosts say media coverage overstated the absolute risk, and note that transdermal delivery appears safer than oral because of liver processing.

segments.title: Early testosterone isolation and famous users
segments.summary: Testosterone was isolated around 1935, and the hosts mention the 1939 Nobel Prize in chemistry for sex hormone work, and a wartime British idea to feminize Hitler with estrogen.

segments.title: Early testosterone use and Michael Dillon
segments.summary: Early testosterone use included an attempt to treat homosexuality, which failed. The hosts discuss trans hormone therapy history and the Michael Dillon episode, and explain their use of sex terminology as a biological shorthand.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: The three estrogens
segments.summary: Estrogen is described as a family of three hormones: estrone, estradiol, and estriol. Their production sites, roles in menopause, pregnancy, and the body beyond reproduction are discussed, including bone, muscle, and brain functions.

segments.title: Estrogen and endurance, skin, and mood
segments.summary: Estrogen's roles in endurance, skin elasticity, brain activity, and mood are discussed, with typical hormone level ranges given for premenopausal women and men. The hosts note estrogen may encourage physical movement.

segments.title: Testosterone and the androgen family
segments.summary: Testosterone is introduced as part of the androgen family, with DHEA and DHT named. The hosts discuss testosterone's presence in the womb.

segments.title: Prenatal development, aromatase, and the male brain
segments.summary: Describes how all embryos are exposed to testosterone, how aromatase converts it to estrogen in female development, and how testosterone-derived estradiol shapes the male brain. Testosterone levels across childhood, puberty, and adulthood are compared, along with hormone complexity and links to male pattern baldness.

segments.title: Testosterone decline with age and bone health
segments.summary: Testosterone declines about one percent per year from the thirties, and it and estrogen both contribute to bone remodeling, with testosterone associated with outer bone and estrogen with inner bone.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Testosterone, aggression, and dog neutering
segments.summary: Discussion of popular associations between testosterone, sex, and aggression, including a Rambo reference. Neutering effects on dog aggression are discussed, with a proposed explanation that testosterone relates more to confidence.

segments.title: Studies on testosterone and violent behavior
segments.summary: Studies of athletes, actors, blue-collar workers and con men showing above-average testosterone, and prisoners with violent offenses showing above-average levels. The hosts note it is unclear whether testosterone drives behavior or behavior changes testosterone.

segments.title: Winning, losing, and local brain testosterone
segments.summary: Winning and losing in competitions shifts testosterone levels, including a 2008 election study of male voters. Testosterone may be released to support a response rather than trigger it, and testosterone produced locally in the brain may influence behavior more than blood levels.

segments.title: Testosterone and libido
segments.summary: Testosterone increases libido in trials, though falling levels do not necessarily reduce sex drive.

segments.title: Intersex people, puberty blockers, and testosterone therapy
segments.summary: Hormone therapy for intersex people and transgender people, use of puberty blockers for precocious puberty and for trans youth, and testosterone replacement for deficiency. Evidence that it improves sexual function more clearly than energy levels. A testosterone supplement advertisement is mentioned.

segments.title: Wrap-up and transition
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the episode, reiterate that listeners should not take their medical advice, and transition to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: school bus yellow
segments.summary: A listener named John Colts writes about the 1931 Pleasant Hill tragedy near Pleasant Hill, Colorado, in which a school bus stuck in a blizzard led to five student deaths and a driver's death, and how this contributed to Colorado adopting yellow buses by 1939 and the later national standard.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and give the show's contact and network information.
